newsitem.title: INDIA: India seen needing to sustain rice export markets.
newsitem.headline: India seen needing to sustain rice export markets.

text.p: India expects a good winter rice crop but the country needs to tap both old and new markets to keep rice exports at reasonable levels, traders said on Thursday.
They were speaking against a backdrop of concern that last year's record sales of more than five million tonnes would nearly halve this year.
"Last year was a windfall," said Rashmi Bhimjyani, a leading Bombay foodgrains exporter.
India exported nearly 5.5 million tonnes of rice in the 1995/96 fiscal year (April to March), exceeding a target of three million.
It emerged as the second biggest rice exporter that year, after Thailand.
Industry officials are concerned that India's rice exports in the 1996/97 fiscal year will dip to about three million tonnes due to lower international demand and uncompetitive prices.
"I would be really happy if we can achieve two million tonnes this year," Mulraj Tanna, another leading exporter, said.
"We should never aspire to meet 5.5 million tonnes. That was an exception," he said.
Tanna said attempts should be made to stabilise non-Basmati exports at around 2.5 million tonnes a year by tapping existing and new markets.
He said the demand for rice from Asian countries this year was lower.
"Countries like Philippines, Indonesia and Vietnam have good crops and are well covered," he said.
Tanna also noted that export prices of Vietnam, a traditional exporter, were $20 a tonne lower, compared with Indian prices for similar varieties.
Traders said Indian five percent broken non-Basmati rice was currently quoted at $300 a tonne F.O.B, 10 percent at $285 a tonne, 15 percent at $275 and 25 percent at $240 a tonne.
Bhimjyani said 1996/97 rice exports would be around 2.0 million tonnes to 2.5 million tonnes, and urged attempts to to sustain these levels.
"Business on the rice front is as usual. Maybe we cannot achieve last year's exports but, compared with 1993/94 and 1994/95, we are doing excellently," he told Reuters.
India exported only around 600,000 tonnes of non-Basmati rice in each of the 1993/94 and 1994/95 fiscal years.
Traders said India's rice harvest was in full swing, with more than 40 percent of the crop already harvested. Winter rice output is likely to be nearly two million tonnes above last year.
The agriculture ministry last week said India's 1996/97 (July to June) winter rice output was estimated at 71.27 million tonnes, up from 69.69 million tonnes the previous season.
India harvests two rice crops, with the bulk of output from the winter crop. Sowing for the winter crop begins in July and the harvest starts from October.
Bhimjyani said India was receiving good enquiries for its rice, and cargoes to East European countries, especially Poland, Hungary and Russia, were moving well.
He said South Africa and Saudi Arabia had shown interest in Indian par boiled rice.
Bhimjyani said lower Indian prices, compared with those in Thailand and the United States, could work to its advantage.
Tanna said business deals were also being negotiated with Iran and some other countries.
"We could sell up to 150,000 tonnes of rice to Iran. The CIS (Commonwealth of Independent States) is annually buying 300,000 tonnes," he said.
Exporters said demand was also building up from Sri Lanka, Ethiopia and Bangladesh.
